newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Havel says joining NATO an obligation for Czechs.
newsitem.headline: Havel says joining NATO an obligation for Czechs.

text.p: Czech President Vaclav Havel said on Friday that the Czech Republic, after bitter historic experience, was obliged to join NATO for the sake of future generations.

Havel, speaking four days before a North Atlantic Treaty Organisation summit in Madrid, said that joining the alliance was a historic opportunity for the country to anchor itself in the European security system which guarded democratic values.

"Given all the bitter historical experiences of this country concerning its former allies, or its pseudo-allies, we see here a tremendous historic chance to get a firm anchor in the security system of Europe," he told Reuters in an interview in Prague Castle.
"It seems to me that it is our obligation to proceed along this line for the sake of future generations."
The Czech Republic, along with Hungary and Poland, are seen as the countries most likely to be invited to join in the first wave of eastward expansion of NATO after the Madrid summit.
In 1968, forces of the now-disbanded Soviet-led Warsaw Pact invaded the former Czechoslovakia to crush the "Prague Spring" attempt to create "socialism with a human face".

"At present nobody threatens the Czech Republic. I am unaware of any foreign troops deployed along our borders and getting ready to invade us but we do not know what will happen 10, 20, 30 years from now," he said.
Havel, who will travel to Madrid for the summit, and other Czech leaders have said that NATO represents the values the new East European democracies share with the West.
He said other organisations, particularly the Council of Europe, had been more involved in developing and guarding these values but said NATO's miltary strength remained important.

"Of all these structures, NATO is the only one that is an instrument capable of serving the needs of collective defence, collective security. And as such it is tremendously important because it helps create stable space for the advancement of these values which it is called upon to defend."
Havel, who led the bloodless "Velvet Revolution" which overthrew Communist power in Czechoslovakia in late 1989, presided over the dissolution of the Warsaw Pact in 1991.
But his presidency expires early next year and he has yet to declare whether he will seek a new term which would allow him to sign the Czechs' accession to NATO, expected in 1999.

"It would be nice if I, as the one who announced in Prague the official dissolution of the Warsaw Pact...signed the accession to NATO, " he said, but added he had not yet decided whether to seek a new term..
"This is a subject to which I shall have to give careful thought but I also know I shall quite soon have to announce the outcome of this thinking," he said.
Havel has said many times that NATO expansion must not end with the first wave and that the alliance should be open to all Euro-Atlantic democracies.
"It should be said clearly that the enlargement process does not end with the invitaion of the first countries," he said, when asked what he expected from the Madrid summit.

"The summit should give everyone hope and assurance and explain in understandable terms why it is not possible to take in all the aspiring nations... It should also articulate the requirements for membership of all aspiring nations."
Opinion polls show fewer than half of Czechs support NATO membership and many people have blamed political leaders for failing to stimulate debate on whether to join.
Havel said politicians alone were not to blame but acknowledged they could have done more.

"I believe that this sort of indifference or lack of interest on the part of the public is not opposition to NATO, it is simnply a manifestation of Czech parochialism, Czech provincialism, Czech isolationism which is not unlike the isolationism of the United States.
"The people simply do not see an enemy and ask why should we invest still in defence or in a defence alliance?"
